title: How to grant camera access in Zoom on Mac: System Settings steps for Zoom Workplace
metaTitle: How to Grant Camera Access in Zoom on Mac, Step by Step
description: How to grant camera access in Zoom on Mac: open System Settings, go to Privacy & Security, click Camera, and turn on Zoom. Steps and fixes.
targetKeyword: how to grant camera access in zoom on mac
intro: To grant camera access in Zoom on Mac, open System Settings, choose Privacy & Security, click Camera, and turn on the switch next to Zoom. If Zoom was already open, quit it and start it again so the change takes effect.
tldr: Open System Settings from the Apple menu, then go to Privacy & Security > Camera.
Turn on the switch next to Zoom. If Zoom does not appear, open it, start a test video, and check the list again.
On the first camera prompt, click OK. Don't Allow turns camera access off until you switch it back on in System Settings.
If Zoom was running when you changed the setting, quit it and reopen it.
The current desktop app needs macOS 10.15 or later.

blocks.text: Zoom asks macOS for permission before it can use your camera. macOS keeps that permission in one list, so you change it once and the setting applies to Zoom everywhere on your Mac. The app is now called Zoom Workplace, but the permission still lives in System Settings under Privacy & Security. This page covers the desktop app on a Mac. If you join calls in a browser, the browser asks for camera access on its own, and you will find that setting in the browser instead. Read on for the exact path, the first prompt trap, and the fixes that work when your video stays black.
Check your macOS version before you start

Start by checking which macOS version your Mac runs. Open the Apple menu and choose About This Mac. Zoom's current desktop app requires macOS 10.15 or later, so a Mac on an older version will not get the latest build. If your Mac runs an older system, Zoom Workplace 6.7.7 is the last release that supports macOS below 10.15. Install that version if you must stay where you are, and plan an upgrade when you can.

Zoom's sources do not agree on this number. A Zoom permissions article mentions 10.14, while the system requirements page says 10.15. Use 10.15 as the working number, and check the requirements page if your Mac sits right on the line. The gap is a single minor version, so confirm your version before you spend time on the steps.
Grant camera access step by step in System Settings

The steps below follow the path in Zoom's official macOS support article. Each screen asks for one decision. The table lists what you should see at each stage, so you can check your progress as you go. Zoom's own video settings choose which camera to use, but they cannot grant the macOS permission. Only System Settings can do that.

A Privacy section with a list of permission types
A list of apps, each with an on or off switch

A question asking whether Zoom can use the camera
blocks.caption: The screens you pass through and the choice on each one

blocks.text: On the Camera page, look for an entry named zoom. The name may appear in lowercase, and that is still the Zoom app. If you use Zoom Rooms, you may also see that entry, and you should turn on its switch too. The switch applies to the app as a whole, not to one meeting, so you only need to set it once.
What the first camera prompt asks you

The first time Zoom needs the camera, macOS shows a prompt. You can click OK or Don't Allow. Click OK and Zoom gets access immediately. Click Don't Allow and access stays off. Zoom cannot use the camera until you switch the setting on yourself in System Settings. That is the only way back, so it helps to know the path before you need it.

blocks.title: Don't Allow is easy to click
blocks.text: The prompt looks like a routine question, and it is easy to click the wrong button when you are in a hurry. If you do, go back to the Camera page and turn the switch on.
When Zoom is missing from the Camera list

Sometimes the Zoom entry does not show up in the Camera list at all. That usually means Zoom has not asked for the camera yet, so macOS has nothing to list. Open Zoom, start a test video, and let the prompt appear. Then go back to System Settings, open Privacy & Security, click Camera, and look again. If the entry still does not appear, quit Zoom completely, reopen it, and repeat the test. A restart gives Zoom another chance to make the request.
Common mistakes that waste time

items: Clicking Don't Allow on the first prompt, then assuming Zoom is broken.
Changing the switch while Zoom is open and never restarting the app.
Looking for the camera permission inside Zoom's preferences. Permission lives in System Settings, not in the app.
Forgetting the microphone. It has its own row in the same pane, so check it too.
Expecting one change to cover every browser. Browsers keep their own camera lists.
Trying the current desktop app on macOS 10.14 or older.

blocks.text: Worked example: fixing the camera just before a call

Say you open Zoom on your MacBook a few minutes before a client call, and your self-view is black. Start with System Settings, then Privacy & Security, then Camera. You find Zoom in the list, and its switch is off. You turn it on, quit Zoom from the menu bar, and open it again. Your face shows in the preview on the next try, and you join the call on time.

Suppose the switch had already been on. The next thing to check is whether another app holds the camera. Close any other video app, restart Zoom, and check the preview again. A camera can only serve one app at a time in most video apps, so the conflict is worth ruling out before you reinstall anything.
Microphone and other permissions in the same pane

The Privacy & Security page lists more than the camera. Microphone sits in the same section, and Zoom needs it to hear you. Check both rows before a call. Change only the switches you need. Turning a switch off for Zoom does not change how other apps behave, and you can turn it back on whenever you like.
Older Macs, the web app, and browsers

If your Mac runs macOS 10.14, the current desktop app is not for you. Install Zoom Workplace 6.7.7 instead, which is the last release that supports macOS below 10.15, and plan to upgrade when you can. The Zoom web app works differently. The browser asks for camera access, so the setting lives in the browser's site settings. Open the browser, find the Zoom site in its camera permissions, and allow the camera there. The macOS steps above cover the desktop app only.
What to do next

Once the camera works, check your audio and video together before the meeting. Open Zoom, start a test video, and check the preview. If you want on-screen help during a call, read the [Zoom assistant page for Mac](/apps/zoom) to see what it can and cannot do. For the wider setup, the [download page](/download) lists the current Mac requirements.

blocks.title: Check before the call
blocks.text: Open Zoom a few minutes early, start a test video, and confirm your face shows in the preview. That leaves time for a restart if you need one.

faq.question: Do I need to restart my Mac after I grant camera access?
faq.answer: Usually not. Restart Zoom if it was open when you changed the setting. Zoom's support article calls out restarting the app as the step that applies the new permission.

faq.question: Why does Zoom appear as zoom in the Camera list?
faq.answer: Zoom Workplace is the current name for the desktop app, and the list entry can appear in lowercase. Look for zoom, or Zoom Rooms if you use that product. Turn on the switch for the entry you find.

faq.question: What if I clicked Don't Allow by mistake?
faq.answer: Open System Settings, go to Privacy & Security, click Camera, and turn on the switch for Zoom. Then quit and reopen Zoom and check the preview.

faq.question: Does this also fix the microphone?
faq.answer: No. The microphone has its own row under Privacy & Security. Turn it on the same way if Zoom cannot hear you.

faq.question: Which macOS version do I need for Zoom on Mac?
faq.answer: The current Zoom Workplace desktop app needs macOS 10.15 or later. Zoom's permissions article mentions 10.14, so check the requirements page if your Mac is close to the limit.

faq.question: Can I grant camera access to Zoom in a browser?
faq.answer: Yes, but the browser handles it. Open the browser's site settings, find the Zoom site in its camera permissions, and allow the camera. The macOS steps on this page cover the desktop app only.

faq.question: Why is my video still black after I allowed access?
faq.answer: Check whether another app is using the camera, then quit and reopen Zoom. The Camera list shows what you allowed, not what another app is doing with the camera right now.

faq.question: Will Zoom ask for camera access again after I allow it?
faq.answer: Not in the same way. Once the switch is on, Zoom keeps access until you turn it off in System Settings. You only need to return to the Camera page if the switch changes or the video fails.

steps.name: Open System Settings
steps.text: Click the Apple logo in the top-left corner of your screen, then choose System Settings. This opens the settings window that holds the macOS privacy permissions.

steps.name: Open Privacy & Security
steps.text: In the System Settings sidebar, select Privacy & Security. The page shows a Privacy section with a list of permission types.

steps.name: Select Camera
steps.text: Under Privacy, click Camera. You see a list of apps that have asked for camera access, each with an on or off switch.

steps.name: Turn on Zoom
steps.text: Find the entry for zoom, or Zoom Rooms if you use that product. Turn on its switch. Zoom can now use the camera once the app restarts.
steps.tip: If the switch is already on, skip to the restart step.

steps.name: Restart Zoom if it was open
steps.text: If Zoom was running, quit it completely and open it again. Restarting the app applies the new setting.
steps.tip: Quit from the Zoom menu in the menu bar. Closing the window alone may leave the app running.

steps.name: Test your camera
steps.text: Start a test video in Zoom, or join a meeting you control. Check that your face shows in the preview before you join a real call.

steps.name: Handle the first camera prompt
steps.text: If Zoom asks for camera access, click OK. Choosing Don't Allow turns the permission off, and you then need to switch it on by hand using the steps above.
steps.tip: The prompt is easy to dismiss by accident, so read it before you click.

troubleshooting.problem: Zoom is not in the Camera list
troubleshooting.fix: Open Zoom, start a test video, and let the prompt appear. Then reopen Privacy & Security, click Camera, and look again.

troubleshooting.problem: The switch is on but the video is still black
troubleshooting.fix: Quit Zoom from the menu bar, reopen it, and check the preview. If it stays black, close any other video app and try again.

troubleshooting.problem: You clicked Don't Allow on the first prompt
troubleshooting.fix: Go to Privacy & Security, click Camera, and turn on the switch for Zoom. Then restart Zoom.

troubleshooting.problem: Your Mac runs macOS 10.14 or older
troubleshooting.fix: The current desktop app needs macOS 10.15. Install Zoom Workplace 6.7.7, the last version for macOS below 10.15, and plan an upgrade.
Make sure you opened System Settings, not an older settings window. Use the sidebar to find Privacy & Security.
